title: Two-file manifest split — global discovery + per-project behavior, no per-project agent.json in v1
body:
The agent-discoverability artifact is split across two files with different audiences and lifecycles:

(1) Global discovery: `~/.dontpanic/agent-manifest.json` answers 'how does an agent find and invoke DontPanic on this machine?' Contains: DontPanic version, install source, CLI path, common commands, MCP server command (once F002 ships), safety rules, project registry pointer, supported intake types, default agent roles. Machine-level — NOT committed to project repos.

(2) Project behavior: `<repo>/.dontpanic/dontpanic.json` answers 'how should DontPanic operate in this project?' Contains: project key/name, plans dir, primary/auditor preferences, test/build commands, protected paths, allowed agents, target env/project references, governance docs, intake defaults. Project-level — committable when secret-free. Legacy `<repo>/.jarvis/jarvis.json` remains read-compatible. **This file already shipped in Phase A's F003 (plan 2026-05-03-001) — Phase B does not touch it except documentation of the rename compatibility.**

No per-project `agent-hints.json` in v1 — explicitly NOT created. Defer until evidence shows agents need a separate repo-local manifest.

Reason for two files, not one: collapsing them would force an OpenClaw-style external agent to re-discover DontPanic per-repo, or force a project to embed machine-level CLI paths that travel with the repo. Different questions, different audiences, different lifecycles. The OpenClaw integration story is about DontPanic being callable, not DontPanic-as-a-runtime — the global manifest is the primary integration surface.

How to apply: F001 lands the global manifest writer/reader. F003 (docs) cross-references both files but does not introduce new schema. Phase C's intake pipeline will read both at dispatch time.

title: MCP intake tool deferred to Phase C — explicitly NOT in F002 surface
body:
F002's MCP server exposes exactly 6 tools: `list_projects`, `validate_plan`, `dispatch`, `status`, `approve_gate`, `read_evidence`. **No `intake` tool.** This is a deliberate scope cut.

Reason: Phase C (intake pipeline) is the most-ambitious phase and will design the brief-to-plan transformation, sufficiency checking, discovery-budget rules, and cost-model implications. Exposing an `intake` MCP tool in Phase B would lock in a contract — input shape, output shape, error semantics — before Phase C has thought through the design. The cost of a premature `intake` contract is much higher than the cost of one extra round-trip when Phase C ships and adds it to the tool surface.

What callers do in the meantime: agents that want to start an intake flow against DontPanic in Phase B's window invoke the CLI directly (`dontpanic intake prd <file>`, etc.) once Phase C ships. The MCP `intake` tool lands as a Phase C feature, not a Phase B retrofit.

How to apply: F002's tool registration test must include a NEGATIVE assertion that `intake` is not in the tool list. The README + ECOSYSTEM.md examples (F003) must NOT show an MCP `intake` call — they show the 6 documented tools only. Phase C's plan will name the new MCP tool addition as part of its acceptance.

title: MCP server is local-only in Phase B — stdio default, localhost only if port-bound, no remote
body:
F002's `dontpanic mcp serve` is local-only. Transport is stdio by default; if a `--port` flag is added, it MUST bind only to 127.0.0.1 / ::1 — never to 0.0.0.0 or other interfaces. No HTTP listener accepting connections from non-loopback. No authentication scaffolding (deferred to a future remote-MCP plan if/when it becomes necessary).

Reason: Phase B's premise is that DontPanic is callable by ecosystem runtimes (OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor). Those runtimes already solve remote agent access — they have Tailscale, SSH, ngrok, GitHub-based workflows, Claude dispatch, etc. Building a DontPanic-hosted remote daemon now would replicate solved problems and create a security surface (auth, rate-limiting, threat-model) that costs months. The right move is to ship the local surface, let the ecosystem use it, and defer remote-MCP until a real demand signal arrives. The threat model for a future daemon is pre-written in `docs/ROADMAP.md` — none of it is built now.

How to apply: F002 acceptance #3 requires no non-loopback HTTP listener in any code path. F002 tests verify by inspecting the server config / failed bind on 0.0.0.0. F003 docs explicitly say 'local-only' in the README quickstart. Future remote-MCP work is its own plan with its own threat model + acceptance — NOT a F002 expansion.

title: MCP mutating tools default to dry-run; require explicit `confirm: true`
body:
The `dispatch` and `approve_gate` MCP tools default to dry-run when invoked without `confirm: true` in the tool input. Dry-run returns the structured intent (which plan, which feature, which gate, what would happen) but does NOT execute the mutation. To actually dispatch a volley or clear a gate via MCP, the caller passes `confirm: true`.

Reason: This is symmetric with the `--force --yes` and `--yes` patterns Phase A's F002 (projects add/remove) established (D008 of plan 2026-05-03-001). Destructive intent is two-flag, not one-flag-with-prompt. In an MCP context where any chained agent could invoke the tool, defaulting to dry-run prevents 'agent autonomously dispatched 50 volleys overnight' failure modes. Operator-supplied tightening: 'Agent-facing docs should say: do not dispatch without user approval' (D007 below).

How to apply: F002 tool input schemas mark `confirm` as Boolean default-False. F002 tests parametric: `confirm` absent / `confirm: false` / `confirm: true` — first two return dry-run shape, third actually dispatches. F003 docs show every dispatch example with the `confirm: true` flag explicit, AND with a callout: 'surface the plan to the user before passing confirm: true'. The dry-run output shape is part of the F002 acceptance contract — agents need a deterministic preview surface.

title: MCP tools refuse arbitrary filesystem paths — registered projects/plans only
body:
Every F002 MCP tool that takes a plan or evidence path resolves it through Phase A's `_resolve_plan_dir` (registered projects only) OR refuses with a structured error. No tool accepts a bare filesystem path that resolves outside any registered project's plan_dir. `read_evidence` cannot read `/etc/passwd`. `validate_plan` cannot validate `/tmp/some-fake-plan-dir/`. `dispatch` cannot dispatch against an arbitrary directory.

Reason: An MCP server is a remote-execution-shaped attack surface even when local-only. A confused or malicious caller could supply paths the operator never intended DontPanic to touch. The registry-as-allowlist approach is the same shape Phase A's F003 used for `_resolve_plan_dir` (Step 4 cwd fallback is gated by file existence + registry resolution failing first). Phase B inherits and tightens that pattern: in MCP context, the Step 4 cwd fallback is REMOVED — only registry-resolved paths are accepted via the MCP surface.

How to apply: F002 implements a `_resolve_safe_path(plan_id_or_path)` helper that wraps `_resolve_plan_dir` with stricter MCP semantics (no Step 4 cwd carveout). F002 tests parametric over: absolute path outside any registered project (refuses), relative path resolving outside (refuses), name not in registry (refuses), bare cwd-relative path (refuses), registered-name-or-path (resolves). The tool surface is constrained to the registry — it is not a general filesystem API.

title: Manifest must be secret-free and regenerable
body:
Two invariants on `~/.dontpanic/agent-manifest.json` (legacy `~/.jarvis/agent-manifest.json` read fallback only):

(1) **Secret-free.** No API keys, no service-account JSON paths, no auth tokens. The schema rejects fields containing `_token` / `_key` / `_secret` (Pydantic-level field-name validation). The `cli_path` field is OK because it's a binary location, not a credential. Sanitization scan against a written manifest must report 0 findings — same regression suite Phase A's F002 / F022 use.

(2) **Regenerable + idempotent.** Re-running the writer with the same inputs (same DontPanic version, same install source, same CLI path) produces a byte-identical file. No timestamps in the manifest body. No nondeterministic ordering of list fields. Operators (or a future `dontpanic bootstrap` helper) can rewrite the manifest from scratch and recover from corruption.

Reason: The manifest is machine-level discovery, not a credential surface. Mixing secrets in would require ACL hardening, file-mode discipline, and a leak-detection threat model that Phase B does not have time for. Regenerable means the manifest is a derivable artifact, not source-of-truth — operators can `rm` it and re-bootstrap without losing state.

How to apply: F001 schema-level field-name validator rejects `*_token` / `*_key` / `*_secret`. F001 tests include a regenerability test (write twice with same inputs, assert byte-identical) and a sanitization-clean test (scan a written manifest with the existing sanitization_check, assert 0 findings). F003 docs explicitly note that operators can `dontpanic manifest init --force --yes` to rewrite at will — no migration step required.

title: Agent-facing docs must say: do not dispatch without user approval
body:
F003 (discoverability docs) AND F001 (manifest `safety_rules` field) MUST include a literal string instructing agent callers: do not dispatch without user approval. Specific wording (or operator-approved equivalent): 'Always surface the plan to the user before calling `dispatch(confirm=true)`. Do NOT auto-confirm.'

This string must appear verbatim in three places:
  - F001's `AgentManifest.safety_rules` field (so any agent reading the manifest sees it)
  - README's 'How agents call DontPanic' section
  - `docs/ECOSYSTEM.md` (already has the OpenClaw caller recipe; add the safety rule explicitly)

Reason: This is the line between 'DontPanic is a useful tool agents call' and 'DontPanic is the agent's autonomous backend'. The product discipline is plan-first / human-approved-first (PRODUCT.md 'Important Product Principle' section). MCP makes it trivially easy for a chained agent to call dispatch; a calmly-worded safety rule embedded in the manifest + every example reduces that risk substantially without requiring runtime enforcement.

How to apply: F003 acceptance #3 makes this string verbatim-required and verifiable by parametric test (grep all three locations for the exact string). If F003 wants to use slightly different wording in different surfaces, the operator must approve the variant at lock time and the test must be updated to match.

title: External directory listings (PyPI, MCP directory, GitHub topics) are evidence-of-readiness, not hard acceptance
body:
F003 ships a publish-readiness checklist (`docs/DISCOVERABILITY.md`) covering PyPI metadata fields, GitHub topic tags, MCP-directory listing requirements, README badges. **Submitting to those external directories is NOT a Phase B acceptance item.** F003 acceptance is satisfied when the checklist exists, items are marked `[ ] not yet submitted`, and the metadata fields needed for future submission are correct in `pyproject.toml` / README.

Reason: External submissions are committment surfaces. Submitting to PyPI as `dontpanic-orchestrate` is a versioning + maintainability promise — once the name is taken, future renames are painful. Submitting to the MCP directory is a public-listing claim — once listed, anyone can install + report bugs. Phase B's job is to make DontPanic ready for those submissions; the operator decides when to actually submit (probably after a real OpenClaw integration validates the surface). Conflating 'ready' with 'submitted' would force premature publish decisions and create a stop-the-line for issues that should be deferred.

How to apply: F003 acceptance language explicitly says 'evidence of readiness, not delivery commitments'. The DISCOVERABILITY.md file uses `[ ]` checkboxes marked `not yet submitted` so it's clear what's done vs queued. Future submission rides a separate operator action — likely a small post-Phase-B housekeeping commit, not a feature in any plan.

title: Plan ID brand policy — committed IDs are durable, drafts use DontPanic
body: Plan IDs and committed plan folder names are durable identifiers. Once committed, a plan ID may be referenced by parent plans, evidence_refs, scripts, audit trails, decision logs, and transcripts. Historical committed plans containing `jarvis` in the slug stay as-is; renaming them requires high-churn cascade updates for low value. Draft or untracked plans should be renamed to use `dontpanic` before they are committed. New plan IDs use `dontpanic` for brand references. Carve-out: `jarvis` remains allowed when it is a load-bearing technical reference, such as work that explicitly modifies `scripts/jarvis_doctor.py`, `scripts/jarvis_orchestrate/`, `JARVIS_*` compatibility env vars, or historical artifacts whose names already contain `jarvis`. Current runtime layout: new installs prefer `~/.dontpanic/`, `<repo>/.dontpanic/dontpanic.json`, `DONTPANIC_HOME`, and `python -m dontpanic_orchestrate`; legacy `~/.jarvis/`, `<repo>/.jarvis/jarvis.json`, `JARVIS_HOME`, `python -m jarvis_orchestrate`, and the `jarvis` CLI alias remain compatibility fallbacks where implemented. Durable memory mirror: `feedback_plan_id_brand_policy.md`.
